knownFor: Bishop in Ireland, a captive from Roman Britain who went back of his own will to the people who had enslaved him. Almost all that is known of him comes from his own two short Latin writings, the Confession and the Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus.
datesNote: Patrick gives no year in either writing. Newport J. D. White, in 1920, gives 389 to 461 as the most recent calculations for his birth and death, and thinks the Confession was written probably not earlier than 454. The Annals of Ulster put his coming to Ireland in 432 and record his death under 457, 461, 491 and 492; the last says he died in the 120th year of his age
placeNote: Bannavem Taberniae in Roman Britain, where his father had a small farm, a place no held text locates; Ireland, where he gives no place for his slavery; the Wood of Foclut near the western sea, named in his dream, which White places in County Mayo; Ireland, where he says he is a bishop
role: Missionary bishop in Ireland; author of the Confession and the Letter

keyWorks.title: Confession
keyWorks.about: his account of his life and his thanks to God, written in Ireland late in his life: the capture at about sixteen, six years as a slave, the escape, the dream of the Voice of the Irish, his work as a bishop, and the charge his own senior churchmen brought against him. It ends: this is my confession before I die. White notes that the title is not an admission of sins

keyWorks.title: Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus
keyWorks.about: written with his own hand against the soldiers of a warlord named Coroticus, who killed his new converts the day after their baptism and sold others as slaves. He tells Christians not to eat with them or take their gifts until they show sorrow and free the captives. No held text says whether any captive was freed

traces: His writings were kept. An incomplete copy of the Confession stands in the Book of Armagh, written between 807 and 846 by Ferdomnach, the scribe of Armagh, and the earliest title for the two writings together, Libri Sancti Patricii, is found there.

The monks of Bangor in the north of Ireland copied a hymn in a manuscript of about 680 to 691, headed the hymn of Saint Patrick, teacher of the Irish. It says the Lord chose him to teach the barbarian nations. The hymn's own date is disputed.
Armagh claimed him as its founder. White reports that Tirechan wrote, about 670, to set out the authority of the church of Armagh over rival centers.
remembered: Later writers add what his own writings never say. Muirchu, who wrote before 699, tells that Patrick prayed that Coroticus be banished from this world and the next, and that the warlord took the form of a little fox. The Welsh History of the Britons, of about 829, makes him a swineherd for seven years, says Pope Celestine sent him, and gives him 120 years. A Life in the fifteenth-century Book of Lismore calls him chief apostle of the west of the world.

uncertain: Almost everything rests on Patrick himself. No independent fifth-century witness names him. Prosper of Aquitaine, a chronicler of his century, records that Palladius was sent as bishop to the Irish who believe in Christ in 431, and never mentions Patrick. So Patrick was not the first Christian or the first bishop in Ireland.
He gives no year. The dates are reckonings by White and the annals, and the annals disagree on his death by more than thirty years. Which of his two writings came first is not known.
He says he baptized many thousands and had church ministers appointed everywhere. The numbers are his own, and he is the only witness to them.

He says only that God made him a bishop in Ireland. He never says who made him bishop, or when. Muirchu names Germanus of Auxerre and the History of the Britons names Pope Celestine; White finds the early evidence against Celestine and calls Patrick's own silence the most telling fact.
He never says what the sin of his youth was, which his senior churchmen brought against him, or how they learned of it. His dearest friend, to whom he had told it, later shamed him in public.
He names no place for his slavery. Tradition says Slemish in County Antrim, and Bury argued for County Mayo; White reports both. Neither is Patrick's own word.

Who Coroticus was is an editors' reconstruction. White, following Zimmer and Bury, takes him for Ceretic, who ruled in Strathclyde about 420 to 450 or later, with his seat at Dumbarton. Stokes says only that he seems to have been a Briton.

briefReferences: Confession 1, tr. Newport J. D. White: Patrick the sinner, the most unlearned and least of the faithful, held in contempt by very many. This is the opening of the brief.

Confession 1 and 2, and Letter 10: his father Calpurnius a deacon, the son of Potitus, a priest; his father a member of the town council; captured at about sixteen with many thousands of others, and the havoc made of his father's servants. Letter 2: soldiers who are by right his fellow-citizens in Roman Britain.

Confession 16 and 17: tending flocks, prayer up to a hundred times a day and nearly as often at night in snow, frost and rain; a voice in his sleep, after six years, that his ship was ready two hundred miles away.

Confession 23: at home in Britain, the dream of a man from Ireland with many letters, one headed The Voice of the Irish, and the cry of the Irish to him as holy boy, in the Wood of Foclut. White notes that adhuc may mean once more or hither.
Confession 37 and 46: gifts offered him with tears to stay; his senior churchmen, who talked behind his back and judged him too unlearned, but did not say it out of malice.

Confession 14, 38, 41, 42, 51, 52 and 55: baptism of many thousands; church ministers appointed everywhere; the children of Irish chiefs as monks and women vowed to God, some against their fathers' will; the slave women who suffer most; kings seizing him and binding him in irons until the fourteenth day; the expectation every day of death or slavery.
Confession 26, 27 and 32: the charge his senior churchmen brought against him, a matter from his youth that he had told his dearest friend, who later shamed him in public. He never names it.

Letter 2, 3, 7, 14 and 16: the soldiers of Coroticus, the new converts killed with the sword the day after baptism, in white, the oil fragrant on their foreheads; others sold; fellow-citizens of demons; no one to eat or drink with them or take their gifts until they show sorrow and free the captives; the comparison with the Roman Gauls who ransom captives from the Franks; the thought that it is a disgrace to them that his people were born in Ireland. Letter 10: born free, a town councillor's son, a slave in Christ to a foreign people.

Confession 43, 59, 61 and 62: his wish to see Britain and Gaul and his belief that he was bound to stay; his prayer to shed his blood with the strangers and captives; the Gospel the only reason for returning; signed in Ireland as Patrick the sinner, unlearned, my confession before I die.
White, Introduction: the Book of Armagh, written between 807 and 846 by Ferdomnach, holds an imperfect copy of the Confession; Armagh and the church that claimed Patrick as founder.
Prosper of Aquitaine, Chronicle: under 431, Palladius sent as first bishop to the Irish who believe in Christ; he never names Patrick.
Antiphonary of Bangor: a hymn headed the hymn of Saint Patrick, teacher of the Irish, copied about two centuries after his time.
Muirchu, Life of Patrick, tr. White: the first Life, written more than two centuries later, whose author admits his authorities are uncertain; the legends of later writers.
World census, Insular / Irish Monastic Christianity: his tradition.

quotationOriginals.modern: I am Patrick, a sinner. I am utterly unlearned, and the least of all believers. Very many people look down on me.
quotationOriginals.printed: I, Patrick the sinner, am the most illiterate and the least of all the faithful, and contemptible in the eyes of very many.
quotationOriginals.work: Patrick, Confession 1, tr. Newport J. D. White
quotationOriginals.original: Ego Patricius, peccator rusticissimus et minimus omnium fidelium et contemptibilis sum apud plurimos

quotationOriginals.modern: We beg you, holy boy, come and walk among us once more.
quotationOriginals.printed: We beseech thee, holy youth, to come and walk among us once more.
quotationOriginals.work: Patrick, Confession 23, tr. Newport J. D. White
quotationOriginals.original: Rogamus te, sancte puer, ut uenias et adhuc ambulas inter nos.
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Latin puer is boy or youth (White: youth). Adhuc is once more or hither; White chooses once more and says it matters little.

quotationOriginals.modern: By birth I was a free man, and my father was a town councillor. I sold my noble rank for the good of others, and I am not ashamed or sorry. In short, I am a slave in Christ to a foreign people.
quotationOriginals.printed: I was freeborn according to the flesh ; I am born of a father who was a decurion; but I sold my noble rank — I blush not to state it, nor am I sorry — for the profit of others; in short, I am a slave in Christ to a foreign nation
quotationOriginals.work: Patrick, Letter 10, tr. Newport J. D. White
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Stokes inserts traditus, handed over, after in Christo in his Latin; it is left out here as an editor's word.
